newsitem.title: EGYPT: Syria says Arabs "not optimistic" about peace.
newsitem.headline: Syria says Arabs "not optimistic" about peace.

text.p: Ministers from Egypt, Syria and the six Gulf Arab states are "not optimistic" about the fate of the Arab-Israeli peace process, Syria's foreign minister said after a two-day meeting started here.
"We discussed the peace process. Our general view in the meeting without exception is that we are not optimistic about the fate of the peace process," Farouq al-Shara told Reuters.
He spoke as he left a meeting late on Saturday of foreign ministers from the Damascus Declaration -- Syria, Egypt, United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman.
The eight countries formed the alliance named after the agreement they signed following the Gulf War in 1991 and meet every six months to keep it alive.
"All the states, members in the Damascus Declaration, they have the same opinion," Shara said.

Syria and Israel have not held face-to-face talks for most of this year. Syria says progress is impossible as long as the Netanyahu government refuses to discuss withdrawal from the Golan Heights, captured from Syria in 1967.
Shara is due to hold talks with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak on Sunday, the final day of the Damascus Declaration's meeting to discuss Middle East peace and other issues.

Syria, the toughest of the eight states towards Israel, was expected to argue that Arab states should respond to the challenge of a right-wing government in Israel by ending steps towards normalisation of relations with the Jewish state.
Egypt's Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said the ministers discussed Middle East peace.

"We talked about the peace process. Farouq al-Shara explained the position of Syria on the peace process, and the lack of movement on this track, and the current stage of negotiations on the Hebron subject," he told reporters.
Asked if the Omanis and Qataris were freezing normalisation with Israel, Moussa said, "Yes, they told us that."

Oman and Qatar went further than other Gulf Arab states in ties with Israel when they said they would set up trade offices there. The other Gulf Arab states have said they want full Israeli peace before any normalisation.
But Oman froze ties with Israel earlier this month and says Israel is not adhering to its commitments to the Palestinians. Qatar put its ties with Israel on hold for similar reasons.
Moussa said they all agreed that "Israeli movement is what is required".
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat is due to consult with Mubarak in Cairo on Sunday amid a flurry of diplomatic activity to wrap up a Hebron deal with Israel, PLO officials said.
Hebron is the last of seven major West Bank towns occupied in the 1967 Middle East war that Israel agreed to turn over to the Palestinian Authority under the 1995 self-rule deal.
Mubarak has said the Hebron agreement could have an impact on the Israeli-Syrian side of peace talks.
Moussa also said the ministers agreed on a joint Arab action plan coordinating economic, security and trade issues.

There was no announcement of any decisions on other issues to be handled by the ministers, including a border dispute between Qatar and Bahrain and the alliance's ties with its main two eastern neighbours -- Iraq and Iran.
Bahrain and Qatar have been at odds for decades over a cluster of small islands and sandbanks in the Gulf, controlled by Bahrain since the 1930s but also claimed by Qatar.
A GCC summit in the Qatari capital Doha this month, boycotted by Bahrain, decided to set up a committee to resolve the rift between the two Gulf states.
Moussa said they all agreed in the meeting to adhere to what Gulf Arab leaders decided in that summit and what was agreed in an Arab summit in Cairo in June.
